skyline.text: Why Amit Varma minds the state knowing what Google knows
Ajay Shah on why single standards breed mediocrity
James C Scott’s state legibility, and why India got it early

footnote.text: UPI does not have a business model.

brief.head: A narrow corridor
brief.text: Where the state wins outright, as in China, modern technology can keep it on top for good, Ajay Shah warned, drawing on Acemoglu and Robinson. {056-C09}

brief.head: My money, my cash
brief.text: Whenever a law says you are not allowed to use cash, Ajay Shah said, he sees a fundamental failure of private property: “It’s my money, it’s my cash.” {#cash}

brief.head: Practice and theory
brief.text: Ajay Shah twice reached for an old line: an economist is someone who, when something works in practice, wonders whether it works in theory. {056-J02}

brief.head: The sound of rivals
brief.text: Signal, WhatsApp and Google Chat are a little incompatible, and we all whine about it, Ajay Shah said. That is how a healthy economy sounds. {#chat}

brief.head: The editor’s hand
brief.text: Raymond Carver wrote much of his work for *Esquire* under the editor Gordon Lish. When they stopped working together, Amit Varma said, Lish’s contribution became clear. {056-S09}

thought.text: Our job in society is to establish a process of discovery, not design.

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on UPI, Aadhaar and the state
lead.head: Paid by phone, priced in freedom
body: Amit Varma still pats his pocket for his wallet before he goes out. But since the hosts arrived for this shoot a few days ago, he has not taken it out once. He pays for everything by phone. {056-S01}

That worries him. He and Ajay Shah have always spoken of cash as freedom, and called demonetisation an attack on it. Yet, he admitted, “it is super convenient to go anywhere, just pay with your phone.”
Friends from abroad tell him India is getting one thing right: what some call DPI, digital public infrastructure, and others DPG, digital public goods. Both terms, Varma said, are flawed.

The technology, he granted, is amazing at a narrow level. But chapters 27 and 28 of *In Service of the Republic*, Shah’s book with Vijay Kelkar, convinced him that the whole logic of the apparatus is flawed.
## Mind the words

Shah, “a Nazi on language”, began with terms. Economists define a public good as non-rival and non-excludable, like clean air. Linux qualifies. UPI, owned by one corporation and closed even to non-banks as full participants, does not. Nor does Aadhaar.
“No, just because a government monopoly does it, it doesn’t become a public good,” Shah said. {056-C01}
His larger target was high modernism, James C Scott’s name for the belief that powerful engineers and bureaucrats can design society from on high. Real life, Shah said, is messier than a whiteboard.

UPI has no business model, so participants never invest properly. Payments fail: once, paying a Delhi traffic fine, Shah saw one fail six times. Disputes go unresolved, and fraud happens on a large scale.
Varma’s objection was simpler: monopoly, state-run or not. With rivals, a system must adapt or go bust. Shah added that the internet itself won by fighting off a government standard.
“Single standards are mediocrity,” he said. “Single standards are the silence of a graveyard.” {056-C05}
## The state that sees

The second worry is power. State legibility, another of Scott’s terms, is the state’s ability to see its people. States have abused such information again and again, Shah said, so every gain needs matching checks and balances. {056-C07}
India issued its first Aadhaar number in 2009 and still has no privacy law. Shah and Kelkar call this premature state legibility.
Defenders say the state could always piece a profile together from twenty databases. At Indian levels of state capability, Shah replied, that was a real barrier, and a single number removes it.
Why mind the state knowing what Google knows? Varma’s answer was one word: consent. Shah’s was: “Google knows a lot about me, but Google does not have coercive power on me.” {056-C10}
## What might have been

The alternative to UPI, Shah argued, was never cash. Had India opened payments to private and foreign players in the 1990s, Moore’s Law would have delivered anyway. Instead the Reserve Bank of India kept rivals out, PayPal among them.

As for the idealists who built these systems, Shah does not doubt their motives. But in public life, he said, an engineer must also be a bit of a philosopher. Varma, once dismissive of such insiders, now wants them inside.
Shah’s parting shot was at the hype. “There is nothing about the Indian development crisis which really will be materially moved by these technologies,” he said.

second.label: UPI fraud
second.head: Savvy, and still conned
second.deck: Ajay Shah on a clever friend’s loss to UPI fraud, and who protects users
body: Ayush Patnaik, whom Ajay Shah calls an extremely clever person, was defrauded of 15,000 rupees through UPI. If even he could be conned, Shah asked, what hope for everyone else? {056-S03}

Over millions of transactions, Shah said, some payments will go wrong. But UPI was designed top down, and nobody settled who takes responsibility or how consumer complaints are resolved. When the payer says the money went and the payee says it never arrived, “there’s really no way to get a recourse”.
On that gap, Shah said, a great wave of fraud has arisen, and the system is not ready for it. {#science} His verdict: “it’s a science project.”

quote.text: And if Ayush got conned out of 15,000 rupees, then imagine what happens to dentists and grandmothers.

second.caption: the friend who got conned

third.head: The PayPal India never had
body: In the late 1990s and early 2000s, Ajay Shah said, PayPal already had what sounds like UPI to Indians: a payment handle such as “Amit at PayPal”, with a backend to send and receive money.

Many Indian exporters were using it to get paid by customers abroad, in what Shah reckoned were billions of dollars. {#paypal} So PayPal asked the Reserve Bank of India to let it run domestic payments too.
“And the Reserve Bank of India blocked that,” Shah said. {056-S05} Even today, he noted, UPI is open to banks only.

The cheers for UPI, he argued, credit a state monopoly with gains that Moore’s Law would have brought through private competition anyway. {056-C11} There would have been five rival systems, and merchants grumbling over which they took. “We should grin and bear it,” Shah said.
third.caption: PayPal and the RBI

p2.title: The case against DPI
p2.deck: Five objections to India’s digital public goods, set out by Amit Varma and Ajay Shah

sections.label: The first objection
sections.head: A monopoly by any other name
sections.caption: what a public good really is
body: If different people start using words in their own strange ways, Ajay Shah warned, “we will get a tower of Babel.” {056-J09}
Amit Varma pushed back: language does evolve, and spontaneous order is the best thing. But where specific terms mean something specific, he agreed, they should not be messed up.
Economists invented the public good, Shah said, and Paul Samuelson laid down the basic theory of clean air as one. {056-J10}

A public good is non-rival: your breathing clean air does not diminish what is available to me. It is non-excludable: it is not even in theory possible to keep a newborn child from it. National security, law and order and the eradication of smallpox fit the bill. So do Linux and OpenStreetMap.
## A finite pipe

UPI does not. It is the property of one corporation, a finite pipe, and highly excludable: not even non-banks are allowed in as first-class participants. Aadhaar is a government monopoly. Governments are supposed to provide public goods, Shah said, but a government doing something does not make it one. {056-C01}

Why the confusion? Shah saw “an element of greenwashing”. Middle-class India cheers for the good words, and criticism starts to sound perverse. “How can you criticise a public good? How can you criticise infrastructure?” {056-C02}
~ Varma offered his own example of a diluted term: “Oh, the market failed to give me a red shirt, it’s a market failure.” {056-J04}

quote.text: Anything that is the private property of one corporation is not a public good.

sections.label: The second objection
sections.head: Designed on a whiteboard
sections.caption: high modernism
body: High modernism, Ajay Shah said, is the idea that powerful scientists, engineers, bureaucrats and politicians design society and send the design down from on high. The phrase appears in James C Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*, though it runs much before the book. {056-R11}

Either we accept it as helpless lemmings, Shah said, or it is backed by coercive power. Amit Varma noted how attractive the label sounds: “it’s modernism, it’s high”. In truth, he said, it is coercive power from the top down.
The real world, Shah said, is a complicated dance of asymmetric information, fraud, crime and consumers with problems to solve. {056-C03}
## A science project
UPI, he said, has no business model, so participants join as nation building. A firm will put on a demo and rub shoulders at a ribbon-cutting. It will not invest seriously without profit. {056-C04}

Monopoly makes it worse. Varma called it the key problem, state or private: with rivals, a system adapts or goes bust. Shah went further. Linux has ten rival file systems, and the United States has 13 or 14 rival companies with their own electronic health record systems. {#ehr}
~ That squabbling, Shah said, is where continuous improvement comes from, and private connectors bridge the gaps. A single standard, by contrast, is “the silence of a graveyard”.

quote.text: The problem with the high modernist idea is it does not adequately grapple with the messiness of the real world.

sections.label: The third objection
sections.head: The state can see you now
sections.caption: premature state legibility
body: Technology, Amit Varma said, in many ways does more for individual liberty than any political movement. But the state can use it to oppress, and in India the balance already tilts its way: “we are effectively subjects and not citizens.” {#subjects}

State legibility, a term from James C Scott, is the state’s ability to see its people. States that amassed information, Ajay Shah said, have abused it again and again, so each gain in visibility needs matching checks and balances. {056-C07}
## Legible too soon

India issued its first Aadhaar number in 2009 and still has no privacy law. {#aadhaar2009} Other countries carried a common-law tradition forward: a policeman who cannot open my letter cannot read my email. India has neither the tradition nor a modern law.
Linking databases was always possible in principle. In practice, at Indian levels of state capability, it was hard, and a single number removes that friction. {056-C08}
Varma recalled that in the case against the activist Teesta Setalvad, the state went through her credit card bills, found she had once bought alcohol, and held a press conference about it. {056-S07}
~ He noted that Rahul Matthan says the state could always get such data by older means, and that Aadhaar does not reveal your bank number. Shah thinks that is not true; they left it for another day.

quote.text: every time the information in the hands of the state goes up, you need to commensurately increase the checks and balances

sections.label: The fourth objection
sections.head: Give Moore his due
sections.caption: Moore’s Law and the monopoly
body: Amit Varma put the common objection. It works, it is convenient, and the common person says, “I have nothing to hide.” Why worry?

Ajay Shah’s answer began with the counterfactual. The alternative was never a world without electronic payments. Had India opened payments to private and foreign players in the 1990s, Moore’s Law would have worked on payments anyway.
Instead the Reserve Bank of India blocked them. So, Shah said, “we are attributing the glory of Moore’s Law on electronic payments to UPI.” {056-C11}
## The magic of flight

His analogy was Air India. Early flights felt miraculous: a plane, heavier than air, and “in thirty minutes I had reached Bhuj.” {#bhuj} That was the greatness of civil aviation, he said, not of a government monopoly. Service improved once rival airlines came in.
His second answer was about time. Many policies feel great in the short run and turn out toxic. India celebrated the Green Revolution, Shah said, but it was done by very bad means. {056-C12}
~ Varma pointed readers to the hosts’ agriculture episode, which shows how bad government policy is partly behind India’s diabetes epidemic.

quote.text: Moore’s Law on electronic payments could have come to us by another channel, which is a private competitive industry with multiple rivals.

sections.label: The fifth objection
sections.head: No engineer is that bright
sections.caption: discovery, not design
body: The builders of these systems, Amit Varma suggested, might say they cannot control whether the state makes them monopolies or uses coercion. They can only build the best system they can. Ajay Shah called this the “I’m a plumber” strain: blame the philosophers of India.

He does not doubt their motives. They are idealists who stepped forward at a high personal opportunity cost to serve the country. {#idealists} But in public life, Shah said, “you can no longer be an engineer. You have to be a bit of a philosopher.” {056-C13}
## No pointy heads

Consumer protection, fraud prevention and the “hundreds of pages of manuals” should not be designed at all, Shah argued. They evolve in a self-organising system, where every day people solve for their own self-interest.
No engineer, he said, is bright enough to design the modern world. Society needs discovery, not design, without “any pointy-headed guy at the top” planning the Republic of India. {056-C06}

~ Varma wants Shah, already a card-carrying engineer and economist, to become a card-carrying political philosopher. If philosophy has failed us, he said, everyone with a voice should jump into the breach.

quote.text: The modern world is more complex than what any engineer can develop.

side.boxText: Amit Varma’s doubts about DPI were once about isolated things, like the coercion in Aadhaar. Chapters 27 and 28 of *In Service of the Republic*, by Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah, showed him that the whole logic of the apparatus is flawed. {056-R01}

contQuote.text: It is almost impossible to envision the emergence of the UK of the Renaissance and the Enlightenment coming about in China today. Because today the Chinese state is on top and it is using modern technology

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Four tales of networks, fines, freedom and the people inside the system

stories.start: Exactly the India digital public goods story play out many years ago
stories.end: BSD and Unix had the correct engine on how to do these things
stories.caption: how the internet beat X.25
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the standard governments pushed, and lost
stories.head: How the internet routed X.25
body: Long before India’s digital public goods, Ajay Shah said, the same story played out in computer networks. The world’s telecom monopolies, many in the public sector even in advanced economies, got together and designed a networking standard called X.25.
Governments agreed to it and private equipment makers fell into line. It was to be the great new global standard. Shah found it “very reminiscent of the top-down push that we see here in India”.

Something very different happened. The United States DARPA had contracted researchers, Vint Cerf among them, to build a standard for battlefield conditions: extremely robust, able to handle failure and reroute dynamically.
That, Shah noted, suits Himachal Pradesh, where the hosts were sitting. A line goes down, a line comes up, and TCP/IP shifts paths and finds a channel through.

Bill Joy and others put TCP/IP inside Unix. Academic computer scientists and hobbyists all over the world built BSD, which later turned into Linux. “So the entire internet revolution came by fighting off a government standard,” Shah said. {056-S04}

TCP/IP also saw off Microsoft, then a large and important computer company with a standard of its own, and Novell, with another. Two giant corporations and one government lost. “And the hackers and the hobbyists and the academicians, they won.” {#won}

~ Why? Brain power and adaptation, Shah said: hundreds of minds all over the world, thinking and rethinking. He pleaded with India’s policymakers and bureaucrats, who he thinks “have failed to understand how engineering happens”.
stories.why: Standards wars, Shah argued, are the sign of a healthy field, not a problem to fix. The internet is the proof: a bottom-up standard, built by many squabbling minds, beat one backed by governments. {056-C05}

stories.end: six consecutive times the UPR transaction failed, it only got through on the seventh
stories.caption: the fine that wouldn’t go through
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah, a Delhi policeman and a payment that stalled
stories.head: Fined in Delhi, failed six times
body: Ajay Shah was stopped by a policeman in Delhi for going through a red light. The fine was not the trouble. Paying it was. {056-S02}
There was a catch. “The cop is saying I will not accept the fine in cash. I will only accept it in electronics,” Shah said, “and the damn electronics doesn’t work.”

Shah had perfect internet connectivity. Even so, the UPI transaction failed six consecutive times and went through only on the seventh, while he sat “grumbling my heart off that this is the state of modern India”. {#fail}

~ Failures are inevitable over millions of transactions, Shah said. But UPI was designed top down, and nobody worked out who takes responsibility when one goes wrong. The user is compelled to use it and has nowhere to turn.
stories.why: A system pushed from the top, with the state forcing its use, leaves nobody on the hook when it fails. Designed systems, Shah argued, handle the mess of the real world poorly. {056-C03}

stories.start: I remember back in the day when I would rant against Shadhar
stories.end: from the very entity which is supposed to protect my freaking freedom
stories.caption: the one-word answer
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on why Aadhaar is not like Google
stories.head: Google asks; Aadhaar doesn’t
body: Amit Varma ranted against Aadhaar and held out against taking it for the longest time. In the end there was no choice: to pay his taxes, he had to do the linkage, and he did. {#taxes}
People often asked him what he thought was a naive question. Why mind giving your data to the government, when you give it to private companies like Google and Facebook anyway?
His answer was always one word: consent. With a private company there are terms of use, he said. He can delete his account. Whatever he shares, he shares out of his own free will. {056-S06}

~ Ajay Shah added a second distinction. Google has no coercive power, and the big tech firms he spreads his life across cannot subpoena one another. {056-C10} The Indian state is unaccountable and already leaks data.

quote.text: It is a blow to my freedom from the very entity which is supposed to protect my freaking freedom.

stories.start: I'd written a newsletter post a while back
stories.end: I would just have been dismissive. Today I want them there.
stories.caption: insiders and outsiders
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on outsiders, insiders and a litmus test
stories.head: The outsider who wants insiders in
body: Amit Varma has always seen himself as the quintessential outsider, an equal-opportunity offender to every party in power. Partly through conversations with Ajay Shah, he came to see that he had sometimes been unnecessarily harsh on insiders.

He still draws a hard line at demonetisation. It was, he wrote in the *Times of India* at the time, the largest assault on property rights in human history. {#demon} Insiders who kept quiet failed a lasting litmus test.

DPI is different, he said. “If DPI is going to be built anyway, if Aadhaar and UPI are going to happen anyway, I would rather have a Viral Shah and a Sanjay Jain and a Rahul Matthan inside the system than outside.” {056-S08}
~ He will keep griping about coercion and the panopticon. But ten years ago he would have been dismissive. “Today I want them there.”
stories.why: Criticism from outside and engagement from inside can coexist, Varma suggested. The skill lies in telling which issues, like demonetisation, demand that insiders speak up, and which reward staying in the room.

quiz.q: What two properties make something a public good, in the definition Ajay Shah used?
quiz.a: Non-rival and non-excludable: your use doesn’t reduce mine, and nobody can be shut out.

quiz.q: How many times did Ajay Shah’s UPI payment of a Delhi traffic fine fail?
quiz.a: Six times in a row; it went through only on the seventh attempt.

quiz.q: Which networking standard, backed by governments and telecom monopolies, lost out to TCP/IP?
quiz.a: X.25, designed jointly by the world’s telecom monopolies and pushed by governments.

quiz.q: What one word did Amit Varma give when asked why Aadhaar differs from Google?
quiz.a: Consent: with Google he accepts terms and can leave; with Aadhaar he had no choice.

quiz.q: Which company, according to Ajay Shah, asked the RBI to let it run domestic payments?
quiz.a: PayPal, which already offered handles like “Amit at PayPal”; the RBI refused it.

quiz.q: What does Ajay Shah’s book with Vijay Kelkar call India’s rapid rise in state visibility?
quiz.a: Premature state legibility: the state sees more, with no matching checks and balances.
